questions.prompt: What does Swift's Law of Exclusivity forbid?

options.text: Two overlapping accesses to the same memory when at least one is a write.
options.explanation: Right. Multiple reads can overlap, but any write requires exclusive access.

options.text: Any function that reads the same variable twice in a row.
options.explanation: Wrong. Sequential and overlapping reads never conflict.

options.text: Creating two structs with the same property names.
options.explanation: Wrong. Struct definitions do not share memory locations.

options.text: Using let constants across two functions.
options.explanation: Wrong. Constants are read-only and never violate exclusive access.

questions.modelAnswer: Swift's Law of Exclusivity says two accesses to the same memory location cannot overlap if at least one is a write. Multiple overlapping reads are safe. Passing a variable as inout starts a long-term write access for the whole call. Any other read or write during that call causes a conflict.

Gives a runtime trap example such as a closure capture overlap or class-stored struct field inout

questions.modelAnswer: Swift rejects obvious aliasing at compile time, such as passing &score twice to inout parameters or calling p.shareHealth(with: &p). Other overlaps pass compilation and crash at runtime with a fatal exclusivity trap. For example, reading a captured variable inside increment(&step) or passing two fields of a class's struct property overlaps at runtime.

questions.modelAnswer: On a local struct variable, the compiler proves that health and energy occupy separate parts of memory, so passing both as inout succeeds. When that struct is stored on a class property like Box.pair, both inout arguments access Box.pair as a whole and collide at runtime. Copying pair to a local variable before mutating fixes the crash.

questions.modelAnswer: Strict Memory Safety is an opt-in Swift 6.2+ check. It warns whenever code calls @unsafe APIs or uses unsafe pointers without marking them. Prefixing an expression with unsafe silences the warning by making the boundary visible for review, like try for errors. It adds zero runtime bounds or lifetime checks, so replacing pointers with Span or InlineArray is safer.

questions.modelAnswer: Swift protects memory in layers: definite initialization, ARC, bounds checking, exclusive access, Swift 6 concurrency isolation, and Strict Memory Safety. In a large codebase, I enable .strictMemorySafety() first on low-level Swift packages that touch C APIs or pointers. Teams mark valid code with unsafe for review, then replace raw buffers step by step with Span and InlineArray.
